drivingQuestion: Does the mishna's rule that a snake on one's heel does not warrant interrupting the Amida extend to a scorpion?
outcomeNote: Rav Sheshet's restriction stands unchallenged within this unit; it is attacked in the following sugya.

segments.he: אֲפִילּוּ נָחָשׁ כָּרוּךְ עַל עֲקֵבוֹ, לֹא יַפְסִיק. אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא נָחָשׁ. אֲבָל עַקְרָב — פּוֹסֵק.
segments.en: We learned in the mishna that «even if a snake is wrapped around his heel, he may not interrupt» his prayer. In limiting application of this principle, «Rav Sheshet said: They only taught» this mishna «with regard to a snake,» as if one does not attack the snake it will not bite him. «But» if «a scorpion» approaches an individual while he is praying, «he stops,» as the scorpion is liable to sting him even if he does not disturb it.

moves.cueHe: אפילו נחש כרוך על עקבו, לא יפסיק
moves.summary: the mishna's snake clause is quoted as the lemma
moves.about: the mishna's clause that even a snake coiled on one's heel does not permit interrupting the Amida

moves.cueHe: אמר רב ששת: לא שנו אלא נחש
moves.summary: Rav Sheshet confines the ruling to a snake and rules that a scorpion permits stopping
moves.about: the mishna's leniency about not interrupting applies only to a snake, which does not bite unprovoked, but not to a scorpion
